doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Advice to young singers: the word and the melody
summary: Brown says she cannot read or scat, admires Ella Fitzgerald and the pianist-singers, and urges attention to lyric and melody.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: A couple of other things I’d like to ask you. If you had some words to the wise, to say to young jazz singers coming up, about the real essence of the music, what would you share?

Well, as I said before, I’m not a technical musician as far as the written note is concerned. But what I have aspired to do, now that I’m being accepted in that gender as a jazz singer in some places, is to first of all as a vocalist, pay attention to what comes out of your mouth, what you are saying, the written word. You know as I say, technically, a lot of people who can read music can just pick up a lead sheet and sing the song. But your job is to make that song apply to someone. Try to be as true to the melody as you can. One of the things over the years I learned in listening to all the great singers, there are a lot of them that I’ve attempted to emulate, but there’s one that I am not stupid enough to try, and that’s Ella Fitzgerald. The lady is without a doubt the greatest that I ever heard, technically. The one thing I never tried to do is scat sing. Even though Ella told me she started that way. She was singing, and forgot the lyric one day, and couldn’t think of anything else to do. So she started to scat. But all the great singers, like Carmen McRae, Sarah Vaughan, my friend Dinah Washington, all of these ladies, Aretha even now, all

played piano. They were musicians. I couldn’t do that. So I had to pay attention to the word and the melody. And I find that to be a source of being able to handle the song. To me if I pay attention to what’s coming out at this point I just attempt to make a person listen to what I’m saying. To make it believable, you know. To have someone come up and say, “You know I’ve heard that song done a lot of times but when you sang it I really felt it,” you know. I think that is the payback for that. A lot of times I have a respect for every music. I can find something in all of it. But there have been some occasions that it gets a little abstract, if I can’t hear the melody, if I can’t hear the, feel the beat, you know? I think that comes from the R&B training that you feel the beat. It’s always there. It’s always there. And when I lose that sometime I kinda, I couldn’t say that I would stand up and be able to sing with Ornette Coleman, you know, I respect him, but I don’t think that I could vocalize. And there is that difference you know. There are a lot of wonderful musicians who are fantastically good in what they do, but very few have a knack for accompanying a singer. There is a difference in accompanying a singer. To give her room, space, for what it is—
